statement: a one-dimensional diffusion model with dynamic Langmuir adsorption and channel narrowing describes the propagation of ALD growth in a narrow channel
an analytic approximation of the diffusion equation makes the model fast enough to fit measured thickness profiles, and the fit yields the adsorption equilibrium constant and the sticking coefficient
the simulations predict the measured profiles of the Al2O3 and TiO2 processes quite well
once a channel is long enough, its length has no effect on the penetration depth
the LHAR gap, typically 500 nm high, is a trench turned sideways inside a pillar-supported polysilicon membrane
the fabricated channel lengths spanned 1–5000 µm (1 µm to 5 mm)
for the typical gap height the length over height gives aspect ratios from 2 to 10 000
experimental conformality data are rare in the ALD literature; four groups are named as the exceptions
earlier LHAR prototypes served the conformality analysis of Al2O3, TiO2 and Ir-based films
fitting the model to a measured thickness profile extracts kinetic growth information; the TMA/water and the chloride TiO2 processes verify it
p_B is the partial pressure of the carrier gas B, nitrogen, in the collision rate of Eq. (1)
Eq. (1): the hard-sphere collision rate of A molecules in an A + B mixture from the diameters, molar masses and partial pressures
Eq. (2): the mean speed of A molecules, (8RT / π M_A)^1/2
Eq. (3): the gas-phase diffusion constant D_A = 3π v_A² / (16 z_A)
Eq. (4): the Knudsen diffusion constant D_Kn = h (8RT / 9π M_A)^1/2
Eq. (5): the hydraulic diameter of a rectangular channel, h = 2 / (1/H + 1/W)
Eq. (6): the effective diffusion constant follows the Bosanquet relation, 1/D_eff = 1/D_A + 1/D_Kn, bulk diffusion and wall collisions in series
Eq. (7): the molecular diameter from the gas viscosity, for common gases
water vapor at 100 °C has a viscosity of 12.55 µPa s
the water molecule's diameter from its viscosity is 418 pm
the viscosity of nitrogen at 11 °C is 17.07 µPa s
the nitrogen molecule's diameter is 374 pm
a rough molecular diameter is enough, since Knudsen diffusion limits the transport in narrow channels
Eq. (8): for ALD reactants without a measured viscosity the diameter follows from the density of the condensed phase
TMA is dimeric at low temperature but above 215 °C more than 96 % is monomeric, so the monomer's diffusion constant is used
the molecular diameter of TMA used in the model is 591 pm
the molecular diameter of TiCl4 used in the model is 703.9 pm

Eq. (9): the saturation adsorption density q follows from the film density, the molar mass of a formula unit, the saturation growth per cycle and the metal atoms per formula unit and per reactant molecule
for TMA and Al2O3, b_film = 2 metal atoms per formula unit and b_A = 1 per reactant molecule
for TiCl4 and TiO2, b_film = 1 and b_A = 1
water molecules, lighter and smaller than the metal reactants, diffuse much faster, so the metal precursor's diffusion is taken as the growth-limiting factor
the gas enters at x = 0 and propagates along the channel by diffusion; the channel is much wider than high, so the concentration is uniform across y and z
the time constant for diffusion across the channel height is about 10 ns for a 1 µm channel, far below the millisecond scale of ALD
the effective diffusion coefficient is typically about 1 cm²/s
Eq. (10): the one-dimensional diffusion equation for the partial pressure with a wall-adsorption sink term g 4RT / (h N_0); solvable numerically but impractically heavy over thousands of pulses
Eqs. (11)-(12): Langmuir chemisorption, adsorption rate (1 − θ) c N_0 p_A / (2π M_A RT)^1/2 with the lumped sticking coefficient c, desorption rate q θ P_d
c is a lumped sticking coefficient that combines every sequential and parallel surface process
Eqs. (13)-(14): the adsorption equilibrium constant K = cQ / (q P_d), with Q = N_0 / (2π M_A RT)^1/2 the collision rate at unit pressure
Eqs. (15)-(16): the net adsorption rate g = f_ads − f_des and dθ/dt = g/q
during a pulse the net adsorption rate is positive, so reversibility does not matter to the model; the TiO2 fit is better with a non-zero desorption probability
the Langmuir model stands in for a surface reaction mechanism that may be much more complicated
Eqs. (17)-(18): at the channel start the surfaces saturate at once and the flow is steady, so the pressure falls linearly from p_A0 to zero at x_s, the front position
x_s is the zero crossing of the linear pressure part, how far the reactant front has come; it grows as the diffusion length, x_s = (Dt)^1/2
D, the apparent longitudinal diffusion coefficient, sets the speed of the gas front; Eq. (20) gives the diffusive gas flow in the linear region
Eqs. (21)-(22): the molecules adsorbed up to x equal the integrated gas flow, neglecting the small unused amount in the gas phase
Eq. (23): the apparent longitudinal diffusion coefficient D from p_A0, H, D_eff, q, T and K
Eqs. (24)-(28): beyond x_t the pressure has an exponential tail; x_t is chosen so the diffusion equation holds there with θ about 0, and is never negative
Fig. 2: the approximate pressure model against the numerical solution of the diffusion equation at four pulse lengths; the fit looks good
Eq. (29): the equilibrium coverage θ_eq = K p_A / (1 + K p_A) when the pressure changes slowly
Eq. (30): the coverage relaxes exponentially with time constant τ = qK / (2cQ) at half coverage; the equilibrium model holds only when τ is much shorter than the pulse, which real ALD often violates
Eqs. (31)-(32): the Langmuir coverage equation dθ/dt = cQp_A/q − (cQp_A/q + P_d) θ and its analytic solution
a fourth-order Runge-Kutta scheme, self-starting and stable, solves Eq. (31); integrating Eq. (32) numerically would take too long
a fit solves Eq. (31) more than 10 000 times; usually 100 time points of about 1 ms suffice, more when convergence fails
Figs. 2 and 3: the approximate model and the numerical solution give practically identical pressures and coverages
Eq. (33): the error of a penetration depth read from a thickness profile is the thickness error over the slope, smallest where the slope is largest, at half thickness
the half-thickness penetration depth x_p is where the film thickness is half its value at the channel start
definition_note: half the thickness at the channel start, the channel start as reference

statement: Eq. (35): after each pulse the model resets a single channel height to H(0) − 2N gpc, both walls growing; the tail therefore thins a little too steeply
Eqs. (36)-(37): the coverages of all N cycles add up and the thickness is s(x) = θ(x) gpc_sat
Fig. 4: thickness profiles after 1000 cycles for four original channel heights; the lowest channel plugs up at its entrance
a 0.2 µm channel is completely plugged at its entrance after 1000 cycles of the reference process
the Gordon model: the gas enters the wide channel as a front of constant concentration with no diffusion along x; Eq. (38) counts the molecules adsorbed per dx on both walls
Eqs. (39)-(40): the saturated front moves at v = F / (2qW)
Eq. (41): Gordon's molecular-flow conductance of a channel of length x and cross-section WH
Eqs. (42)-(43): the front equation separates and integrates to x + 3x²(1/H + 1/W)/16 = C H t
Eqs. (44)-(45): with C = p_A0 N_0 / (2q (2π M_A RT)^1/2) the Gordon penetration depth at pulse length t_p is H ((1 + 3Ct_p/4)^1/2 − 1) / 0.375 for W much larger than H
in the Gordon model the aspect ratio reached, x/H, does not depend on the channel height
Fig. 5: the penetration depth in one pulse by the numerical solution, the analytic approximation and the Gordon model against pulse length
the Gordon model gives a good penetration depth here, slightly faster since it uses Knudsen diffusion alone, but no thickness profile and no growth kinetics

The Langmuir adsorption model stands in for a surface mechanism that may be much more complicated; the fitted c and K are its lumped parameters.

The model updates one uniform channel height after each pulse, so the modelled tail is too narrow and the film thins slightly too steeply there; fine while the film is thin against H and grows little beyond x_p.
Only the metal precursor's diffusion is modelled; water is taken as never rate-limiting.
The molecular diameters of TMA and TiCl4 are rough estimates from the condensed-phase density; TMA is treated as its monomer.
The thickness precision is about 3 nm, set by how rough the channel surface is.
In the Fig. 5 comparison the Gordon model uses Knudsen diffusion alone, slightly faster than the Bosanquet effective diffusion of Eq. (6).
The approximately 50 nm film thickness is the planar value the sequence leads to, stated without a measurement.
